newsitem.title: USA: N. England Investment sees lower US stocks growth.
newsitem.headline: N. England Investment sees lower US stocks growth.

text.p: The U.S. stock market, coming off a rousing two-year bull run, should post modest growth of five to 10 percent this year, according to Scott Pape, portfolio manager of the New England Capital Growth Fund.
"I am optimistic about the market in 1997," said Pape. "However, gains for the overall stock market in the next year should be rather modest (five to 10 percent) compared to the previous 24 months."
But fellow managers, reflecting the investment disciplines of their funds, offered divergent views on the direction of stock and other markets at a press briefing here on Tuesday.

Contrary to an increasingly prevailing view that U.S. stocks are "fully valued," Pape remains optimistic equities still have upside room. He cited favorable conditions, including low inflation, corporate earnings remaining strong, and continued muscular cash flows into equity mutual funds.
Pape, whose $179 million fund has about one-third of its assets in emerging growth stocks, still sees buying opportunities in the sector.
Fellow manager Helen Young Hayes, of the $72 million New England Star Worldwide Fund, said she was concerned about the potential for slowing profit growth in the U.S.

Hayes likes the business services sector, including Hays Plc, the U.K. provider of staff recruiting and office support. Another favorite is Novartis AG, the drug giant formed from the merger of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz.

John Wallace, manager of the recently launched New England Star Small Cap Fund, said, "It is tough to be exceeding bullish on the market after two great years...History suggests a small up...or even down...year in 1997."
Wallace remained bullish on the technology sector, citing a slew of new company product cycles.

He said that he expected that stocks in the Russell 2000 small stock index to see gains this year. He acknowledged the concerns of other small-cap managers that there was less liquidity among small-cap issues.
Dan Fuss, manager of the $550 million New England Strategic Income Fund, was optimistic on the direction of fixed income securities.

"Over the next year, it looks like bonds could outperform stocks," Fuss said. "I expect the sizzling stock market to cool this year. It appears that corporate profit growth is slowing but not going to be negative."
Fuss said he was "less bullish, but still positive" on emerging market debt in Mexico, Argentina, Brazil and Poland.

Fuss said he expected that the "unusually wide discrepancy in yields between bond sectors should return to more normal relationships." He said that yields of lower-grade bonds could rise compared with those of higher quality.
He said he favored Canadian provincial debt, especially Manitoba and British Colombia, and Thai Euroconvertibles.
New England Funds is a unit of New England Investment Cos LP, which has a total of $100 billion under management, including $24.8 billion in mutual funds.
